analysis.one_liner: Restricts feeding human antibiotics to livestock to keep the drugs working in people.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to the Senate HELP Committee on June 27, 2013, and it sat there until the 113th Congress ended without a hearing or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require drug makers to prove that antibiotics given to livestock in feed or water for growth promotion or routine disease prevention pose no risk of breeding antibiotic-resistant bacteria that can sicken people. Drugs used in human medicine, like penicillin and tetracycline, could no longer be routinely fed to cattle, pigs, and poultry unless the maker showed reasonable certainty of no harm, with existing approvals withdrawn on a two-year phase-out. It would also restrict using these drugs for 'nonroutine disease control,' limiting mass feed-based dosing. The bill was introduced by Senator Dianne Feinstein with 13 cosponsors, including one Republican, and was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who depend on antibiotics working: anyone who gets food poisoning, pneumonia, a skin infection, or a hospital infection, and whose treatment depends on these drugs remaining effective. The bill's own findings cite resistant infections costing society tens of billions of dollars a year and note that 80 percent of antibacterial drugs sold in the U.S. go to food animals rather than people [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who relies on antibiotics working

how_it_helps.text: It would require drug makers to show a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' from antibiotic resistance before a medically important antimicrobial could be approved for nontherapeutic use in food animals, and to withdraw existing approvals after a two-year phase-out if that showing is not made [S2] [S3].

It would ban feeding these antibiotics to healthy animals for growth promotion and feed efficiency, reserving the drugs for treating sick animals and tightly limited disease-control situations [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings cite FDA data that 80 percent of antibacterial drugs sold in the U.S. in 2010 went to food animals, plus studies linking resistant Salmonella, Campylobacter, and E. coli in food to animal antibiotic use and annual U.S. health costs of resistant infections estimated in the tens of billions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large livestock producers and the animal drug industry would bear the cost: they could no longer use cheap, routine low-dose antibiotics to fatten animals and compensate for crowded conditions, and would instead pay for veterinary oversight and alternative practices. The bill's findings cite a Danish ban that produced only a modest increase in production cost [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Livestock producers and animal drug makers

drawbacks.text: Livestock producers would face higher costs from the phase-out, and the bill's own findings acknowledge production costs rise under such bans, though the Danish experience it cites showed only a modest increase and little change in animal health [S3].

Restrictions on mass 'nonroutine disease control' dosing could make it harder to contain outbreaks on crowded farms in some situations, which is why the bill allows feed-based dosing only when a specific, non-customary disease risk on the premises can be shown [S3].

Enforcement would fall on FDA to conduct risk analyses and withdraw long-standing drug approvals within two years, an administrative burden the agency had previously avoided, which critics could point to as either an overreach or an unfunded mandate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is strong and well-documented in the bill itself: preserving antibiotic effectiveness protects everyone, while the costs fall on a concentrated industry and appear modest based on the Danish precedent. The main honest caveat is that the mandate gives FDA a two-year deadline to re-review dozens of old drug approvals, and tighter limits on disease-control dosing could squeeze some producers during outbreaks. On balance the benefits to public health clearly outweigh the costs to the livestock and animal-drug industries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 113th Congress ended, so no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened [S5] [S1].

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on June 27, 2013, joined by 13 cosponsors including Senator Susan Collins, the only Republican [S4] [S5].

The same day it was introduced, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no further action on it for the rest of the 113th Congress [S5].
No hearing, markup, or roll-call vote on the bill appears anywhere in its action history, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Livestock producers and animal drug makers kept the ability to sell and use medically important antibiotics for growth promotion and routine disease prevention without having to prove those uses are safe. Public health advocates, who had spent years pressing for restrictions, gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Livestock producers and animal drug makers

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call; its sponsorship was 13 Democrats and 1 Republican, suggesting potential bipartisan support, but no vote ever tested it [S4].

industries.note: They would lose routine low-dose antibiotic use for growth promotion and feed efficiency, practices the bill's findings show were used on roughly 83-84 percent of swine, cattle, and sheep operations [S3]. Their cost savings from crowding compensation would end, and consumers would gain food less likely to carry resistant bacteria.

Approvals for nontherapeutic uses of medically important antibiotics would be withdrawn after a two-year phase-out unless makers proved no resistance risk, eliminating a major market segment — FDA reported 13.5 million kilograms of antibacterial drugs sold for food animals in 2010 [S3].
The bill expresses the Senate's preference that antibiotic use in livestock occur under a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship, expanding professional oversight work for veterinarians [S3].
